speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I beg to move "That the total sum to be allocated for Head J of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has lived with relative peace and prosperity ever since.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While some parts of the world community were quick to condemn the aggression and breach of international law, this cry was not universal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Every time an act of aggression takes place without consequences for the aggressor, the more each country has to fear for its own safety.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are also worrying developments closer to home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The strategic rivalry between the US and China is intensifying.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Recent incidents, such as then-US Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan and the more recent shooting of China’s hot air balloons over the US have upped the ante, resulting in the cancellation of diplomatic meetings that could have facilitated constructive dialogue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There have also been more military exercises in the Taiwan Strait, one of the traditional flash points in the relationship.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both countries have also doubled down on the implementation of exclusionary measures, especially in the trade and technology spheres.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the strategic competition worsens between the two major powers, Singapore may be caught in the cross-fire.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In addition, middle powers have also taken a greater interest in our region and started to develop more robust strategies to grow their presence in the Asia Pacific.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While many of these are friendly nations, with the growing number of such powers seeking to establish a foothold here, the regional security environment could become increasingly contested and busier.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the Korean peninsula, North Korea has conducted further ballistic missile tests, drawing swift condemnation from neighbours South Korea and Japan and many parts of the world community.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Japan, which had remained a generally pacifist nation since World War II has started to remilitarise in response to the rising military pressures around it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I had earlier highlighted the major geopolitical and security developments that have shaped the environment around us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When the war broke out, many believed that Russia would quickly overwhelm Ukraine and take over.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But instead, what has happened is that Ukraine has put up a spirited and vigorous defence, and they have gotten support, at least in terms of the equipment and finances from powers around them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With both sides unwilling to yield, the war will likely persist for some time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although quite far away, we should monitor events unfolding in Ukraine and Europe.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Russia-Ukraine war has had spill-over effects, which have fundamentally changed the global order.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of these include the hardening of military alliances such as the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) which have now awakened and started growing again and increased defence spending amongst European countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Russia for its part has announced the suspension of its commitment to the New Start Treaty which the US and Russia entered into to stop nuclear proliferation amongst the two largest nuclear powers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This may restart the nuclear arms race, which has been suspended since the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the war continues, there may be more unintended and unexpected consequences that countries, including Singapore, have to deal with.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, as mentioned by the hon Mr Vikram Nair, today marks the first anniversary of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, an act that many did not believe would happen.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has tipped the world order on its head and underscored the importance of upholding international laws and frameworks and, of course, defending national sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a stark reminder for all of us in the world and especially for small states like ourselves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is therefore ever more critical to review our own plans and priorities in diplomacy and in defence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Regional powers are becoming more confident and assertive.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do we navigate relations with our neighbours while being acutely aware of the great power rivalry also playing out in our backyard?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Threats and asymmetrical warfare have evolved as well.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, the recent incursion of an alleged PRC surveillance balloon into US airspace and its subsequent shoot down by the US military underscore growing friction between Washington and Beijing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This comes after the large-scale PLA military exercises bracketing Taiwan following the then US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taipei.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These actions follow increasing PRC military activity in the East and South China Seas and near Taiwan in recent times, to which other militaries, including those of the United States, are mounting their own activities in response.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Prime Minister, and more recently the Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister, have noted rising tensions between the United States and the PRC, which play out over a range of issues and wide swathes of territory.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Manila recently pointed to the PLA Navy using lasers on the Philippine Navy vessel in the disputed South China Seas waters, supposedly blinding crew on the bridge temporarily.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These incidences and growing cleavages do not have anything directly to do with Singapore, at least for the moment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, they could well affect Singapore and our interest in significant and potentially negative ways.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have little doubt that our professional foreign service officers at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are working very hard to encourage some amicable solutions and searching for means to mitigate risks for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Through careful diplomacy in the event tensions should further escalate, this reinforces efforts to support international law and accepted rules of the road that have facilitated Singapore's prosperity, safety and stability for so long.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Nonetheless, I am mindful of the very real possibility that diplomacy law and institutions sometimes may not be enough.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These could potentially be in jeopardy in the event of a major contingency involving the United States, the PRC and others that may occur around our region.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such an event could also spell political and military pressure on Singapore to provide or deny access to one party involved in a crisis or another in addition to broader disruption.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such pressure and disruption may take physical even kinetic form and not just be limited to information, cyberspace and political influence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What is being done to enhance such capacity in recent times, noting that much of Singapore investment in our professional military and national service has historically focused on the Army?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Although I am greatly encouraged by the recent announcement of the appointment of our first Chief of Defence Force from the Republic of Singapore Navy (RSN).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Apart from capacity, I would like to ask what preparations are in place to potentially sustain operations at longer distances from our shores.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This may be important if we wish to prevent and perhaps minimise any dangers to Singapore and Singaporeans in the event of some major emergency in our region.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some people may well, see such concern as unnecessarily alarmist or dismiss them as remote and unrealistic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But as a nation, we must be prepared and vigilant for issues that may be looming to avoid any unwanted surprises, especially in these uncertain times.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Countries understand that they can no longer take their security for granted.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, Japan is stepping up its defence spending and seeking to move beyond 1% of its GDP too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It goes without saying that the US and China have consistently expanded their annual budgets and will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could the Minister for Defence tell us what some of the global trends in defence spending are?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given our small size and vulnerable position, how will these spending trends affect Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has consistently and continuously invested in defence over the last five decades to ensure we have a strong military force capable of a robust defence.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are trade-offs and opportunity costs as a result of our efforts to sustain our commitment to defence.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have persisted, despite the challenges, as we are cognisant that Singapore, as a small island-state, can neither take its own defence for granted nor count on others to defend us.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of our pioneers were sacrificed when Singapore quickly fell to the Japanese in 1942 when Great Britain was distracted by events in Europe.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, upon our Independence, our founding leaders heavily prioritised national defence as they were keenly aware that without ensuring our own security, there would be no future for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A recent MOF report states that the Government will need to make further moves to boost revenue.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These fiscal pressures will continue, given the uncertain economic conditions, our ageing population and rising costs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Building a strong and advanced military is even more so.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Being a small country, it is more challenging for us to negotiate prices for weapons and such as we do not have the economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given these developments, could the Minister for Defence please tell us what will our defence spending look like in the coming years?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the projections for defence spending this year?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will spending return to the past baseline following the impact of COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MINDEF does explain that operating expenditure includes the payments for the purpose of military equipment, maintenance of equipment and camps, allowances for National Servicemen (NSmen) and salaries of regular servicemen and women.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I understand the need for military secrecy, can MINDEF minimally provide the estimated expenditure for just these four items.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a common practice in public budget estimates in other territories, including Taiwan, Latvia and Finland, all of whom face real and existential threats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) conducts scrutiny of the Government's expenditure and accounts, including the defence budget.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, does the PAC have access to any breakdown of military expenditure?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If not, it will be difficult for the Committee to scrutinise the defence budget, given that military expenditure comprises almost 95% of the Ministry's total budget.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairman, for the last few years, we spoke about SAF's transformation into a next-generation defence force by 2040.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To achieve this, SAF has been investing in technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), unmanned systems, robotics and data analytics.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Beyond enhancing assets, SAF is also transforming the way it is organised.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Last year, SAF set up the fourth service – the Digital and Intelligence Service (DIS) – to provide enhanced intelligence, advanced connectivity and resilience cyber defence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: SAF has also set up a new Army "Sense and Strike" headquarters to help the SAF perform better in battle with less manpower.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, SAF must also factor in rapidly changing warfare.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, we should consider how the recent events such as the Russia-Ukraine War has changed warfare; we should also consider how to tap on the growing trends of adopting quick, low-cost adaptation of civilian technology, like Starlink systems and drones into warfare.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In short, even as SAF has built a strong foundation, and has a good transformation plan, we must always make sure that we adapt our plans to evolving realities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, can Minister for Defence provide an update on how SAF is enhancing our capabilities to build our Next Generation SAF?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While such violent conflicts may seem far from our realities here in Singapore, they serve as a stark reminder that we must be able to defend ourselves and deter threats that may come our way.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The war in Ukraine has shown that even in the age of hybrid warfare and grey zone tactics, conventional warfare remains a real possibility.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had to appeal for tanks, fighter aircraft and long-range heavy weaponry from its allies and partners.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, the digital terrain has become as real as the air, land and sea domains.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Financial Times had reported on Russia’s use of malware to infiltrate Ukrainian government and financial systems to create disruption in the early days of the war and even to disrupt crucial satellite connectivity.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The SAF must therefore maintain its ability to deter and defend against threats in both the physical and digital realms.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At last year’s Committee of Supply debate, Minister for Defence Dr Ng Eng Hen talked about the SAF’s transformation efforts to meet future security threats and challenges.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad that we have taken incremental steps to build up and transform the SAF over the years, not just to meet current security threats, but also to anticipate potential new threats that we may face in the future.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can MINDEF provide an update on the progress of the SAF’s transformation?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Alex Yam, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are now living in the digital age.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is no denying that we are bound together in the metaverse.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This poses great opportunities for the world economy but also great challenges and even in the field of security and defence, we are seeing more and more threats emerged online.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The threats of the physical world are now, therefore, manifest in the digital battlefield.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have seen it in Ukraine with large scale online campaigns against Ukrainian, assets as well as those of their allies in Europe.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this vein, I applaud the foresight in forming the Digital and Intelligence Service, the fourth service of the SAF.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What is the assessment of the Ministry of the current digital battle terrain and what threats have been prevented or disabled since the formation of the DIS?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How does the DIS work in tandem with civilian agencies like CSA?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And, how can the DIS bring ordinary citizens on board to play a part in improving cyber security?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the problems are digital, the solution still lies in the real world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What is the manpower situation for the DIS?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, how has the take-up rate been for the NS Digital Work-Learn Scheme in partnership with NTU, which is due to start in April of this year?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will MINDEF encourage more to come on board DIS?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition, what have been the advantages of the unified command so far and how will the DIS strengthen its work with the three other services and other security agencies to ensure that while we keep Singapore safe in the physical world, we also keep our citizens and our infrastructure safe in the digital one?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has revealed the might and widespread use of cyber-attacks as an extension of warfare into the digital space, affecting critical infrastructure that not only impacts military efforts but also the lives of civilians.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These attacks have devastating aftermath on communities, be it in the form of mass power shutdowns in times of harsh weather conditions or in the form of propagating false information to destroy unity or morale.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Ukraine alone has suffered a threefold growth in cyber-attacks over the past year.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The Cyber Peace Institute reveals that as of 17 February 2023, there have already been 627 cyber attacks on government entities and corporations in critical infrastructure sectors, excluding attacks on Ukraine and Russia.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Last October, MINDEF established the Digital and Intelligence Service (DIS) with an eye on dealing with threats to Singapore’s security in the digital domain.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This was a more than welcome development, to build on SAF’s abilities to defend Singapore on multiple and emerging fronts.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To fulfil its mandate, the DIS will need a highly-skilled and collaborative digital workforce to continue to grow Singapore’s digital defence capabilities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, there is fierce competition for such talent in the technology sector.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Can the Ministry of Defence share how DIS plans to attract appropriate talent to the service as well as how recruitment for the DIS has progressed since its establishment last year?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The nature of warfare continues to evolve going into the 21st century.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Unlike the past, battles today are no longer fought in the traditional physical domains of the sea, air, and on land, but also in cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We will also need to contend with another dimension – the rapid pace of technological evolution and disruption, which will also shape the texture of war and future conflict, and thus have a critical impact in shaping the SAF’s military doctrines and future battlefield tactics.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This has the crucial benefit of reducing the risk of losing lives by combatants.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I have been a big supporter of new technologies, particularly unmanned battle platforms and even automated warfare.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: During last year’s Committee of Supply debate, the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) unveiled further plans to build up the Next Generation SAF.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: How will the SAF use these new military technologies as it continues to develop?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Colleagues, Mr Speaker, this Committee of Supply (COS), we sit together with the rest of the world coming out of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have learned to live with the disease and are returning to normalcy.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But it is also clear to all of us that the world has changed, and some things will never revert to the status quo ante.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Among them, hybrid work patterns, greater digitalisation, increased vulnerability of supply chains, rising protectionism.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Many of you have spoken about the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and in parallel, that and rising US-China tensions, which many of you touched upon, are seminal forces that will impede, if not unravel, globalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There is also the potential of physical disruption to key sea lines of communication.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The South China Sea and the Straits of Malacca and Singapore are indeed vital waterways.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Coupled with these external forces, internally, many countries see their citizens pushing against globalisation and immigrants.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The rise in extreme right parties is a vivid sign of this inward-looking mood.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: President of the World Economic Forum Børge Brende recently described our world as one which is gradually sliding from a period of cooperation to a period of intensifying global competition.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: China’s ascension into the World Trade Organization (WTO), if we cast our minds back, was in 2001, so some 22 years ago, where US President Bill Clinton at that time spent political capital to get his Congress to support it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They wanted to speed up China’s transition to a market-based economy for it to be more globally integrated.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As the thinking went, if China was more like the rest of the world, trading with it and co-dependent, then surely Communism as a form of government would be weakened.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: More than 20 years later, I suspect that some within the US and their Western allies, in retrospect, might think that was a mistake.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because China has indeed risen economically and is now one of the largest trading nations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, for the very reasons you push for China to be included in the WTO, it has succeeded.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But just recently, Czech President-elect Petr Pavel asserted that China was “not compatible with Western democracies in their strategic goals and principles”.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The world’s second-largest global trading partner is not compatible with you.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, it is not what you do; it is what you are.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These forces run deep and will alter the very foundational pillars of countries and their relationships with others.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is inevitable, even for large and middle powers, let alone tiny Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And many of you asked what these structural forces, what these tectonic plates will do to us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Alex Yam, Mr Don Wee, Mr Dennis Tan, Mr Vikram Nair.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For Germany, that long believed and worked for the integration of Europe and Russia, those hopes have all but evaporated.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Germany downsized its Bundeswehr, its military, in the 1990s to reap the so-called “peace dividends” after the Berlin Wall fell.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Chancellor Olaf Scholz’s Zeitenwende speech in 2022 marked, as the word means, the end of an era and a turning point.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Closer to home, Asian countries too are upsizing their militaries, especially in Northeast Asia.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members can refer to them and also access the handouts through your MP@SGParl mobile app.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the past decade, Japan’s military spending, albeit as a self-defence force, has been on the same level as France and Germany’s, around US$50 billion every year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Two percent of Japan’s GDP would be around US$85 billion today.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If that happens, South Korea will spend as much as Japan today.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Similarly, Australia will reach these levels of defence spending by 2030.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: ASEAN is not a military pact, but in comparison, spends in aggregate about what one of the ASEAN+8 countries spends – South Korea.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Taken together, and if these facts bring to your minds that Asia is spending a lot militarily, you are quite right.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Taken together, Asia’s military spending on the whole had already surpassed Europe in 2009.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: EU countries will now be spending more because of the Ukraine invasion, but Asia’s military spending will be still larger for some time to come.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All of us of course are asking, as some of your questions alluded to – what will all this lead to?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But without a robust framework to maintain peace, this upsizing of Asian militaries can spell trouble ahead.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some of you know that there is a metaphorical Doomsday Clock that has been ticking away.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is no wonder that some of us sleep less soundly at night.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Here, it would be remiss of me as Minister for Defence if I did not thank Members of this House for their constant and strong support through the years for my Ministry’s budget.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The record shows that Members of Parliament of all political parties and Nominated Members of Parliament in successive Parliaments have shown this collective support.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: None of them were beguiled or rendered complacent by peace to push for less defence spending.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Yes, questions were asked about how MINDEF and the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) put our defence dollars to use and if it was effective, accountability, so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Questions that needed to be asked and were asked by Members here.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Outside this Parliament, some political personalities did push for reduction, saying our defence spending is "excessive”, or that external threats for us "don't exist”.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To them, I say, do not sacrifice a strong defence for Singapore at the altar of political expediency.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It may win some support, but it risks losing Singapore in that self-interest.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew reminded us even in his later years, “Without a strong SAF, there is no economic future, there is no security”.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is a hard truth that remains constant.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We must never forget that defence is a long-term business.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the SAF, major systems and platforms take 10 to 15 years to conceptualise, build and integrate into our fighting force.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is assuming everything runs smoothly, without chop and change.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If a military loses a capability and wants to build it back, it may take twice as long.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We need to remind ourselves constantly that investing steadily in defence is the more prudent and cost-effective strategy, especially during good times and peace.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because it is not just the dollars spent, but the know-how, the human capital, the culture and most important of all, the psychology and mental build-up of commanders and soldiers, crucial for the SAF, which is made up of NSmen in the majority.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some of you have asked what have we learned from the war in Ukraine?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because it is the only war in which modern state-on-state warfare has been fought in recent years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There are indeed military lessons to be learnt.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But more important than military lessons, examples of how people, ordinary citizens make the crucial difference, not only in civilian affairs but military too.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ukrainian civilians have played significant roles in the conflict from the very beginning.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Workers cut up old train tracks and welded them together to create obstacles.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These were known as “steel hedgehogs” – nobody taught them how to do it – and they put them up to block Russian military trucks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Volunteers produced, repurposed and operated drones for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And in particular, when Ukraine’s imports were disrupted and prices of lithium batteries went up and soldiers needed to communicate, volunteers started donation drives to collect and recycle batteries to power drone operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: More recently, we saw footage of improvised grenades reportedly made by the Ukrainian Army in partnership with civilian engineers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Basically, it shows a fragmentation grenade fitted with a shuttlecock that is attached for stabilisation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The grenades could then be lifted by commercial drones and dropped onto targets from above.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A cheap and creative solution, perfect for recycling used shuttlecocks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ukraine’s Armed Forces relied heavily on civilians to gather military intelligence through crowdsourcing.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When the invasion began, the government added new features to the Diia app, it is the equivalent of our Singpass.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And through a chatbot, citizens could help the military locate Russian troops and vehicles by providing photos and videos together with live locations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As footage flooded in, there were multiple reports of Ukrainian troops successfully destroying Russian convoys, thanks to the tip-offs from the public.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There was another crowdsourcing app followed, it is called ePPO, and this was for citizens to report sightings of cruise missiles and kamikaze drones.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is how sophisticated their system had become.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Passion, grit, bravery, innovation, even pure genius in the face of overwhelming adversity.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ukrainians had no electricity or running water, endured freezing temperatures, constantly under the threat of incoming missiles, but the resolve of the Ukrainian people to protect their country, to defend their freedom shone through, through all the misery that war brings.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If the war has taught us anything, it must be that weaponry and fighting platforms are important, but ultimately, it is the fighting spirit of the people that will decide if they end up subjugated or sovereign.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We Singaporeans must build and have that same spirit and resolve.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our lives and our country will depend on it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MAS has estimated that core inflation should come in at 3.5% to 4.5% in 2023.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, we are catching up of projects deferred or disrupted – for example, SAFTI City, NS Square, the delivery of our submarines.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Third, we are spending more on digital and other non-kinetic capabilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: By design, as Members have noted, MINDEF does not give detailed information in the Budget Book.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is not in our security interest to do so, just as we do not give the detailed cost figures for acquisition of planes, submarines and Army platforms because they provide an indication of our capabilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Similarly, we do not want to provide an aggregated amount for the acquisitions – because you can guess – if your capability development is this budget and it is collected over years, what are you spending it for?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But the key question, I think, that the Member Gerald Giam is asking is how then do you assure prudence and accountability of your spending?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Like all public agencies, we are held to account for the management of funds.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are subject to independent audits by the Auditor-General's Office (AGO), where deep dives are taken into processes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In other words, you do not get to see the aggregated picture but you can see any of the individual processes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For example, AGO had discovered payment errors of flexible benefit allowances in FY2021 and these were promptly recovered.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF does not have any say to what the AGO wants to look at.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If it wants to look at platforms, we have to show the detailed processes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As Mr Giam said, the Public Accounts Committee can also request for additional information after examining AGO's audits, as it did in this case.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have strong internal controls to ensure that expenditure is within stipulated ranges of reference costs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In other words, when we pay for something, we take reference from other known quoted figures.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When there are large-scale projects, we have senior management committees to ensure oversight and compliance.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But I take the point – there is a necessary trade-off between accountability and full transparency.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But I think overall, Singaporeans – with an NS Army – can see what our dollars go into and, as I said, the detailed processes are subject to audit.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Barring increasing tensions or persistently high inflation where military spending may have to go up, MINDEF expects this to be the steady state spending.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I will repeat that because my officials are very nervous about this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have stabilised between 3% and 4% of the GDP.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And barring increasing tensions or persistent high inflation, we expect this to be steady state spending.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, this means that over the past few decades, because we have matured, as a percentage of GDP, we have been spending less.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The final accountability – what have we done with all these defence dollars?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked about this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We can have a quiet satisfaction that the SAF today is recognised as one of the most advanced in Asia.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think Mr Dennis Tan asked – what are you preparing to make sure that your sea lines of communication, your airways, towards 2040, how are you preparing?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some perspective: the SAF is not large relatively.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There was a reason I gave that the military spending for all the countries around us.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But for our size – all our Services, we are the most advanced in Asia.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Together, these Services can prosecute campaigns across a spectrum of security challenges.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It has taken two decades but has been completed successfully.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As a result, the Army now uses digitalised fighting and support platforms – the Hunter Armoured Fighting Vehicles, HIMARS and Leopard Tanks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Air Force's Smart Multi-Role Tanker Transport aircraft and Aster-30 Missile Systems are new additions, together with the F-15s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Navy has brought on a full fleet of Frigates and new Littoral Mission Vessels.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the next decade, more platforms and capabilities will be added.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I previously informed this House in 2019 that our Air Force would purchase four F-35 Joint Strike Fighters because we wanted to evaluate it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It allowed us access to information and facilities for a full evaluation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our pilots have flown in F-35 mission simulators.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They have flown in simulators and learnt from operational F-35 pilots.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They have evaluated the electronic systems on board and made trips to F-35 bases to study how other users maintain their fleets.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have also flown with other F-35 operators, in particular, very recently, in Exercise Pitch Black in Darwin, Australia.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All of these have given us valuable insights.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF and the SAF have concluded that the F-35 is the best choice to meet our defence needs now and in the future.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the Navy, we have launched our second and third Invincible-class submarines a few months ago in Kiel, Germany.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Later this year, you can expect the first submarine to return home base.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is, most of the time, underwater, unless you are at Changi Naval Base, where you can see some of it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These custom-fitted submarines will be stealthier, more agile and will remain submerged for a longer period.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This significantly enhances naval capabilities to protect our interests at sea.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At the recent Munich Security Conference, they said, "You have got new Type-218SG submarines." I said, "Yes" – quietly.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the Army, the next-generation Howitzer and Armoured Tracked Carrier will be introduced as well as more unmanned aerial and ground vehicles in our combat units.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some of you ask about future threats – Mr Alex Yam, Mr Henry Kwek.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Indeed, this was the reason we started the DIS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It has allowed us to consolidate military intelligence and digital and cyber capabilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Most of you ask for updates, including most Members of Parliament.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have talked about an SAF digital range.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will contain virtual replicas of networks and systems that we have nationally so that we can simulate a wider range of cyber-attacks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will be used to train our DIS forces and conduct exercises with other military and commercial partners and we will organise joint training with other national agencies – I think Mr Alex Yam talked about that – to defend our critical infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some of you ask what our cyber agency DIS' mission is.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Digital threats in the cyber arena are pervasive daily – literally tens, if not hundreds of thousands.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: What our cyber agencies are more concerned with are external and orchestrated attacks by non-state and state actors, for example, terrorist organisations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The DIS has picked up some entities and is monitoring them for their activities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is as much as I can say.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The DIS will also set up the Digital Ops-Tech Centre, run by software engineers and data scientists, to provide in-house software development.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I am giving you discrete dates and these are our targets.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Recruitment – some of you have asked this – including Miss Rachel Ong.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In 2018, we launched a Cyber Work-learn programme and last year, a new Digital Work-Learn Scheme.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A significant number of applications are for non-uniformed roles.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I think it is doing quite well.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This transformed quadri-Service SAF will provide Singapore with a strong core against foreseeable threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But even so, I agree with many Members here that we must prepare for new disruptive technologies as well as scenarios that we have not seen.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The future is still evolving but the overall shape is discernible.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the not so distant future like many Members talked about, militaries will use a new generation of hypersonic missiles, lethal autonomous platforms and directed energy weapons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Unmanned platforms are now commonly used in both civilian and military settings.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: What will be a game-changer is when these unmanned platforms from air, land and sea are scaled to large numbers and weaponised.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have already seen it in the Ukraine war.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A few years back, drone strikes from Azerbaijan took out Armenian air defences, artillery and armoured vehicles from above.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Recently, in Sevastopol, Ukraine launched a coordinated drone attack against the Russian Navy – nine from the air, seven from the sea.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These drones were able to break through multi-layered defences around the port and damaged at least two Russian ships.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These concrete examples that Members of Parliament have shared are rewriting the doctrine and practice of modern warfare as we speak.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, how does MINDEF and SAF deal with this, I was asked.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Well, we set up organically and organisationally the Future Systems and Technology Directorate (FSTD).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is literally called that – the Future Systems and Technology Directorate.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In it are SAF planners, DSTA engineers and DSO scientists.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Their job is to ignore vested interests in the present SAF but instead to be insurgents, to render obsolete if they can current platforms, forces and even organisations by producing improved ways for Singapore to defend itself in the future.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They do not have that many friends because they are trying to steal somebody's lunch literally.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And if they can show they can do that, then they have succeeded.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our future literally depends on them performing their tasks well.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As an example, FSTD spearheaded the research and investments in unmanned platforms and this was a decade ago – even before what we talked about today.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Today, autonomous technologies will be built into the Navy's new Multi-Role Combat Vessels to function as a "mothership", with unmanned platforms that can work together across a range of missions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This was a decade ago because that is how long it takes to conceptualise and build.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, while older RSN ships typically operate one unmanned system, these vessels are able to operate multiple systems simultaneously.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is one more last vital ingredient for the SAF – our people.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We can have the best platforms and systems in the world, but as the Ukrainian spirit showed, it is the spirit and the know-how that will determine if the SAF can defend Singapore and its interests successfully.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is an infographic on how we are training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In order to have well-trained soldiers, we have to invest and we have invested heavily in our training infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SAFTI City – we have announced it in 2017 – is making good progress.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The completed training circuits will include battlefield effects simulators that can replicate smoke and blast effects and interactive targets that can fire back – a far cry from our days when it is "bang, bang, bang, bang, I shoot you, you shoot me".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We just assume that both did not get shot or both got shot.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This one, cannot "play play", no bluffing, because you wear electronic sensors.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If your platform is hit, that is it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Buildings and roads can be configured so that the soldiers can encounter a different layout each time they train at SAFTI City, so that they can train in a complex urban environment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Surrounding SAFTI City, we will build three new Instrumented Battle Circuits (iBACs).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These circuits will simulate energy fires such as artillery bombardment and air strikes, and they will help our soldiers hone their operational instincts and tactical fundamentals.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The new training facilities will have sensors and video cameras to capture data and provide instant replays.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, you say you shot him, he says he shot you.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Professional sports teams know the value of this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Soldiers and units will receive real-time feedback on their performance and this will help them stay alive, or remain alive.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have also invested large sums into overseas training facilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I visited our soldiers in Australia last year in the Shoalwater Bay, and some of the facilities like the Urban Operations Live Firing Facility and the Combined Arms Air-Land Range will be ready for use from next year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This will allow our NSmen and NSFs to participate in Brigade, even Division-level exercises.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have also increased the use of advanced training simulators, up to 20% additional live training will be replaced by them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You can combine simulators now for different platforms.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But even with all this, we will have to conduct some training locally.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because if COVID-19 taught us something, it is that our overseas training facilities can be terminated instantly and we do not want to be dependent.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I know that Members of Parliament, especially living in the housing estates do get feedback and complaints from residents about noise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we try to mitigate the impact of this noise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Air Force reduces flying tempo during critical exam periods, but there is a limit to that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Help explain to your residents that just like NS, this local SAF training is the price we pay to ensure a credible force to protect our freedom and independence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I visited Luke Air Force Base, where our F-16 squadrons were training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We do to those communities as we do here, we have open house, we treat them to makan, and I was talking to the mayor.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I said to the mayor, "Please tell your residents that we appreciate them tolerating all that noise." It is not as if Luke Air Force Base does not have housing estates.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we fly together with the US planes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And he says, "Don't worry, I tell them this is the sound of freedom." The mayor in Arizona, in Luke Air Force Base, telling his residents, that this is the sound of freedom.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They are willing to invest in our freedom.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I want to thank Mr Chairman and Members for this indulgence for staying on a Friday night.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, can I take the two cuts together?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In order to prepare our National Servicemen (NSmen) to effectively defend Singapore against evolving threats, our training facilities need to be consistently refreshed to make sure that they provide realistic and relevant battlefield environments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Today, the battlefield may not necessarily be in a field or a jungle, but also in an urban environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With Singapore having entered into an endemic COVID-19 phase and gone to Disease Outbreak Response System Condition (DORSCON) Green, can MINDEF provide updates on the SAFTI City and the development of other military training facilities in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many Singaporean soldiers have had the privilege of participating in SAF training overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For these soldiers, this was one of the highlights of their training and service to the nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Overseas training is critical in bolstering our national defence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It allows us to overcome our natural space constraints and conduct important training that would have otherwise been impossible here.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For our national servicemen, it is also an opportunity for them to appreciate the scale of the SAF's capabilities and operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Such overseas training is critical to SAF building up capabilities beyond what the limited space of Singapore can provide.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When will our soldiers be able to utilise this training asset fully?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, Sir, multiple residents have given me feedback about the Republic of Singapore Air Force (RSAF) flying activities in Western Singapore, for example, "They fly so low we can even read the numbers and logos on the planes." "Makes it impossible to work from home or have conference calls." "They blast their engines at 6.20 am and 9 pm." "My young kids get startled by the noise and cry." "We have stayed in the area for over 20 years and have never experienced this intense frequency of noise." One, we all understand that the RSAF must stay operationally ready, so it must train.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Two, airspace in Singapore is tight and the RSAF must fly over residential areas en route to international air space.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And three, some of the flying is, in fact, not training in nature, but operational responses to situations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But can the RSAF review its flying parameters on timing, flying altitude, frequency, and most importantly, its flight path, say if there is a possibility to fly more over the lesser populated Lim Chu Kang area, to ensure a more sustainable balance, in the longer term, between operational readiness and a tolerable level of noise for residents in the West?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairman, Sir, vigorous training is key to an effective military.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Consider combined arms warfare, a modern warfighting concept used by the best militaries, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It involves the combination of infantry, artillery, armour, air support and naval forces.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It requires high coordination and communication between the branches.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Units must be able to work in concert with others, adapting to changing battlefields.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To acquire such sophisticated warfighting skills, our soldiers must train effectively to acquire individual or sub-unit skills.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They must also participate in larger-scale trainings and exercises to build teamwork between units.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, the application of technology can improve the realism and effectiveness of training.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These technologies include individualised or combined simulators for our air, land and sea assets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This also includes war-gaming software and specialised training facilities embedded with sensors and playback capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The challenges we face in the information and cyber domains have grown far beyond any single country's ability to address.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Not only have they grown in relevance, countries are also becoming more reliant on social media and digital technologies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Almost every aspect of our lives has an online presence, including for the purposes of accessing essential services, transactions and communication.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Losing access to the cyber and information domains would be extremely disruptive and is a challenge that transcends national boundaries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: While the world has become more seamless, integrated and interconnected through digital means, it has led to a new wave of modern security challenges, increasing our exposure to cyberattacks, disinformation and misinformation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We have witnessed a significant increase in the volume, frequency and reach of disinformation and falsehoods, not just within, but also across societies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we begin to step out from COVID-19, we are seeing the slow return of things to their normal pre-pandemic state.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we have not been fortunate to witness a similar turning point in the regional security environment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Instead, we see a hardening of tensions and an increasingly charged geopolitical environment, overlaid by deepening UNited States (US)-China strategic rivalry.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Recently, the spy balloon saga has caused the rift between them, to further widen and divide the global community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In last year's Shangri-La Dialogue (SLD), there was a comment by a representative of China's People's Liberation Army of his perception that the forum is dominated by the US and its allies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can Singapore position itself as the neutral platform for open and honest dialogue on regional security?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad that the SAF has resumed its full-scale overseas training exercises in 2022, after two years of COVID-19 disruptions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These overseas exercises are essential to provide our SAF troops with realistic and effective training, given our land constraints.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But this "return-to-normal" also makes training safety a paramount concern, especially where existing National Service (NS) commanders may not have the necessary experience from the last two years of lower-tempo training.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The large majority of our soldiers are full-time National Servicemen (NSFs) or Operationally-Ready NSmen (ORNS).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can all agree that in peacetime, we owe it to their parents and families to return them home after training – safe and sound.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is also my hope when my sons grow up and serve their NS in future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Training safety is often seen to be at the expense of training realism and operational efficiency.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whether through its Inspector General's Office or the External Review Panels on SAF Safety, how has the SAF sought to innovate so that training safety is being pursued together with the aims of operational realism and effectiveness, and not simply enhancing safety measures at all costs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are MINDEF and SAF regularly engaging with foreign counterparts regarding approaches to training safety, and what are some of the useful lessons we have learnt or can learn from other militaries?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, the safety of our service men and women is paramount.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: At last year's Committee of Supply (COS), Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How spoke about emphasising a strong safety culture in the SAF through audits and inspections.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What were the recent findings from such audits and inspections, including those conducted by the External Review Panel on Training Safety?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NS is an important component of our nation's defence and the contributions and commitment of our NSmen are instrumental in ensuring peace, stability and security of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, Singapore's total fertility rate, which is already one of the lowest in the world, is declining.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As a result, the number of full-time NSmen is projected to decrease.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This further exacerbates the situation as our NSmen form the bulk of our defence force.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This statistic could be worrying for MINDEF and the SAF, as it poses a significant manpower and structural challenge to the SAF.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We would eventually have to face the issue of maintaining an effective military force with a much leaner SAF.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chair, many in this House would agree that our people are our most important resource.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our rapidly ageing population and low fertility rate have a direct impact on SAF.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, we must ensure that our NSmen are deployed efficiently to tasks which they are able to carry out effectively and safely.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the adoption of cutting-edge military technologies, there are now new tools that our NSmen can use in a wider range of vocations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is, therefore, timely for us to reconsider whether there are now new opportunities for our NSmen to take on.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would MINDEF, therefore, provide an update on the implementation of these functional assessments?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, the COVID-19 pandemic has caused major disruptions to our economy and society.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In particular, the education, training and opportunities for our young people had been impacted.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many lessons and training programmes were conducted online, and our youth were not able to harness the full benefits of in-person interactions and hands-on experience.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Technology is changing the way we live and work.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding the global layoffs by major technology companies, digital skills – such as coding and data analytics – will continue to be crucial in the future of work.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important that our young NSmen are adequately prepared to meet the challenges of the new economy, even as they train to defend our nation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, MINDEF's Work-Learn Scheme is well-placed to meet the aspirations of our people.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can MINDEF provide an update on the expansion of the Work-Learn Scheme for NSFs to more roles and vocations?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I am heartened by Minister's response to my Parliamentary Question on the subject matter for vocation and choice for our NSFs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The examples he shared ranges from air defence, artillery, intelligence, island defence signals and transport.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This certainly makes the NS period more meaningful for Singaporeans who got their vocation choices, instead of dragging their soles to report back to camp during the duration of NS.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I am speaking on this from my own personal experience in the past when I served my NS.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Can Minister enlighten if any NSFs have decided to pursue a career in MINDEF when they were posted to their choice vocation?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: What is the probability of NSFs having a career in combat as compared to non-combat related?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: With regard to transport that was mentioned in his response, does this include engine technicians or the equivalent?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: What kind of career can the NSF look forward to, should they choose to be in engineering as compared to combat?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that the sophisticated combat vehicles can entice young Singaporeans to take the opportunity to have hands-on experience in the engines of such vehicles.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Allowing NSmen to use their civilian expertise to contribute to national defence should provide for a more effective SAF and a better NS experience.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: After serving their NS, many Singaporeans go on to fulfilling careers in various specialisations, some of which may be valuable to the SAF.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We should consider how best to tap on their skillsets and specialisations, and enable them to make better use of their time during their ORNS.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would MINDEF share an update on whether the number of expertise-based redeployments has gone up and in which areas are they contributing to?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many Singaporeans now enjoy the flexibility of remote working and catching up with friends online has become more commonplace.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many NSmen use their mobile phones connect to their family, to their friends and colleagues.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And these phones also serve as their calendars, wallets, bus and MRT cards.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I would say not just NSmen, but all of us as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But for many of our young NSmen, the digital life is the only life they have ever known.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Given that our NSmen devote precious time to serve the nation, it is necessary for MINDEF to make the best use of technology to ensure that the NS' administrative processes are efficient and convenient.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, may I ask how is MINDEF leveraging technology to improve NS administrative processes – particularly to cater to the preferences of a young and digitally-savvy generation of NSmen?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, our NSmen make many sacrifices to defend our nation, while they juggle NS obligations with the other demands in their work and family lives.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Ensuring an efficient and convenient NS Experience would be most helpful to them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I appreciate the OneNS initiative which seeks to achieve this goal by centralising NS transactions and services, such as SMART Information and Communications Technology (ICT) onto this one-stop platform.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I understand that OneNS can anticipate the needs of each individual serviceman and personalise digital services, so that each can have easy access to relevant information and services in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The NS experience not only consists of two years' full-time service but also regular reservist call-ups in the years that follow, to ensure that the NSmen's skills and knowledge remains relevant and current.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is also a whole-of-society endeavour because families and employers play a huge role to support our NSFs and NSmen whenever they are required to answer their call of duty.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Most importantly, NS is about strengthening Singaporean's commitment and ability to defend and protect Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: To mark the 55th anniversary of NS last year, MINDEF organised a series of activities to recognise the contributions of our NS past and present.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The activities were designed to raise awareness of NS, promote fitness, and highlight the sacrifices and dedication of NSmen over the past 55 years.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The NS55 celebrations also provided an opportunity for the nation to come together to show its support and gratitude to NSmen and their families.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, last year, we commemorated 55 years of NS.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This was a meaningful opportunity to pay tribute to the contributions of our past and present NSmen.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Their contributions and personal sacrifices have ensured the SAF has remained strong, and have kept Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While NS55 activities have concluded, recognition and support for our NSmen should continue.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our Singaporean sons devote two full years of their time, away from their families and loved ones, for the defence of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They put their studies and career aspirations on hold and serve with passion and commitment.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: After full-time NS, our NSmen continue to make sacrifices juggling family, work and NS commitments.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was, therefore, glad to hear that the NS Review Committee had prioritised recognition and support for our NSmen as one of the Committee's three thrusts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I appreciated that Senior Minister of State for Defence Mr Heng Chee How talked about NS recognition in his COS speech last year, including about the enhancement of the NS HOME awards.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can MINDEF and the SAF better support our NSmen's families as well?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would first like to thank our NSmen for being a key pillar of Singapore's national defence.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is important for us to ensure that NSmen and their families are supported and recognised for their sacrifices.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should not take these contributions for granted.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, NSmen have to balance their professional and personal lives alongside their NS commitments during their reservist years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some of them even have to set aside life milestones.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our growing freelance and self-employed workforce often face livelihood losses for each day that they are away from work and, hence, steps to alleviate unnecessary administrative processes will go a long way in helping with the balancing of their commitments.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should seek to continually improve the NS system, so that each and every NS man can have fulfilling and meaningful NS experiences.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should strive to increase conveniences for our NSmen by reducing administrative burdens for them where possible, without compromising on SAF's operational readiness.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One instance of this was in 2019 when Senior Minister of State Mr Heng Chee How announced that ORNS would no longer have to notify the authorities when they travel abroad for less than half a year.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In the war's early days, the world watched with bated breath as the machinery of Russian warfare rolled into Ukraine.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Would the Ukrainians be able to hold, and if so, for how long, how many days?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: One year on, however, the Ukrainians have defied the strong odds against them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Soldiers have fought bravely and valiantly on the battlefield to preserve the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their homeland.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: But we have to look beyond the traditional battlefield too.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Indeed, the total attack nature of modern warfare today has expanded the realm of the traditional battlefield.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Wars are no longer just conflicts between armies, but between nations and their peoples, and how to break their spirit and psychological unity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: On this count, the Ukrainian people have, too, fought bravely against the chaos, destruction and horrors of war.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Instead of buckling under pressure, the Ukrainians came together and rose to the occasion.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Tales of Ukrainians from all walks of life banding together have hit the headlines time and again, displaying inspiring acts of heroism, resourcefulness and ingenuity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: From engineers building portable stoves out of old refrigerator parts to fend off the cold amid power outages, to housewives fashioning makeshift but effective tourniquets and weaving camouflage nets as covers for military vehicles and soldiers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Singaporean actor Ix Shen, who was living in Ukraine, recounted how Ukrainians who lined up in a supermarket to stock up on necessities made way for soldiers and gave them words of encouragement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, at the COS debate last year, Senior Minister of State for Defence, Mr Zaqy Mohamad shared that a "2021 Total Defence Review" was undertaken and had reflected sentiments of Singaporeans wanting space to contribute ideas and efforts towards shaping Singapore's Total Defence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: During the same debate, I also raised the question on how we can continue to engage our youth in defence matters.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The Senior Minister of State then shared about the launch of the Total Defence Sandbox.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Also, the plans to ensure that Total Defence remains relatable and resonate with all Singaporeans?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: An important goal of Total Defence is to build resilient communities; communities that are able to withstand, respond and bounce back quickly from adverse situations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This has never been more critical in this era of uncertainty; politically, economically and also in the form of natural disasters.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: There are examples we can look to, which showcase the strength of a community banding together.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As shared by some, the Ukrainian people have been a remarkable example of a people coming together to not only defend their country, but innovate in the face of great difficulty.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Tech professionals in Ukraine used their talents to aid the nation's efforts and support humanitarian needs amid the crisis, such as creating apps that notify users about bombings or supporting humanitarian needs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Civilians with tech know-how found creative ways to adapt commercially, and to build drones and materials for military use.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Businesses like Headway, a Ukrainian start-up, continued operating from bomb shelters in the midst of air raids, successfully offering bite-sized learning on an app used by 15 million people in over 140 countries.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Others continue to attend and showcase their new innovations at international trade shows.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In the words of a startup founder from Ukraine, Mr Nazar Trokhymchuk: "the militaries are fighting, Ukrainian business is working, start-ups are developing, so everyone is doing their job".

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Chairman, every Singaporean has a part to play in our whole-of-society effort to build a strong, secure and cohesive nation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: New threats continuously emerge, while existing threats evolve and re-invent themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How has MINDEF partnered the community to strengthen Total Defence?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, last year, the World Economic Forum recognised the contributions of one Ukrainian, Fedir Serdiuk, who had founded the First Aid Special Training, or FAST, organisation in 2016 to provide first aid training to ordinary Ukrainians.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: I hope that Singaporeans continue to be inspired by such stories and that more Singaporeans are encouraged to learn about how they can prepare themselves to respond in the event of a national crisis.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: What are the measures planned to increase participation and the range of skills learnt by each participant?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, the global crises in the last two years served as important reminders that the people of Singapore need to be prepared to step up and respond in the event that we face crises.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war has shown the importance of prepared and willing citizens who are able to not only respond to challenges such as food and energy shortages, but also resourceful enough to put lifesaving skills and other civil defence responses into practice, to save their own lives and that of other citizens.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, the COVID-19 pandemic, where not only our healthcare, border security and livelihoods were put to the test, but also the spread of misinformation and disinformation to make things worse.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Three, the recent massive earthquakes in Turkey and Syria, causing thousands dead and missing, and millions displaced.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
